issues.legal_issue: A party may rely on a case supported by the evidence despite deficiencies in the form of its pleadings when the substance of the case was known and litigated without prejudice.
material_facts: The claimant described the school’s occupation as being under a licence.
The school’s managers pleaded that the premises had been permanently given for school use and that the school had made substantial additions and alterations at its own expense without objection.
The trial court framed issues concerning whether the licence was irrevocable, and both sides presented evidence on those issues.
The claimant called the former owner as a witness to support the contention that the licence was revocable.
issues.conclusion: The challenge based on the alleged absence of adequate pleadings failed because the pleadings, issues and evidence showed that the claimant knew and contested the case being advanced.
issues.legal_principle: Material facts must ordinarily be pleaded so the opposing party knows the case to meet, but pleadings receive a liberal construction and their substance, rather than their form, governs. Where the parties knew an issue was involved and led evidence on it without prejudice, a deficiency in the pleadings does not prevent the court from deciding it. The Court relied particularly on Bhagwati Prasad v. Shri Chandramaul, [1956] 1 SCR 286.

predicates.is_appeal_from_possession_suit: A claimant appealed after a court dismissed a suit seeking possession of property occupied by another party.
predicates.opponent_knew_the_case_to_meet: The opposing party’s pleadings or the course of trial made the substance of the other party’s case known.
predicates.issue_was_litigated_with_evidence: The parties proceeded to trial on the issue and presented evidence about it.

issues.definition: When a possession-suit appeal concerns an issue that the parties understood and litigated with evidence, a deficiency in pleading form does not bar a decision on that issue.

issues.legal_issue: A licence may be irrevocable where the licensee, acting on the permission and for its granted purpose, makes permanent works at its own expense with the grantor’s knowledge and without any agreement reserving revocation.
material_facts: The owner informed the education authority that the school premises were given rent-free as a permanent contribution, after which the school received recognition.
The school was permitted to occupy both the building and the attached open land to run the school and impart education.
To meet the need for additional accommodation, the school constructed classrooms and other facilities and incurred expenses, and it also modified and repaired the existing building.
The owner remained involved in the school’s management, knew of the works and raised no objection to them.
The record disclosed no reserved right to revoke, and the purchaser acquired the property while the school occupied it.
The school continued to carry on the educational purpose for which it had been permitted to use the premises.
issues.conclusion: The licence was irrevocable while the school continued the educational purpose for which it had been granted, and neither the former owner nor the purchaser could revoke it to evict the school.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 defines a licence as permission to do on another’s immovable property something that would otherwise be unlawful, without creating an easement or interest in the property. Section 60(b) makes a licence irrevocable where the licensee, acting upon it, executes work of a permanent character and incurs expenses; the section is not exhaustive, and the parties may also make a licence irrevocable by express or implied agreement inferred from purpose, conduct and circumstances. Sections 62, 63 and 64 address deemed revocation and the licensee’s rights following revocation. The Court relied on Gujarat Ginning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Moti Lal Hirabhai Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd., AIR 1936 PC 77, and distinguished Shankar Gopinath Apte v. Gangabai Hariharrao Patwardhan, [1977] 1 SCR 411; it also referred to Jagat Singh v. District Board Amritsar, AIR 1940 Lahore 18, and Thakur Prasad v. J. Thomkinson, AIR 1927 Oudh 206.

rule.if: is_claim_to_recover_property_from_licensee and permission_was_granted_for_a_continuing_purpose and licensee_made_permanent_works_on_the_property and licensee_incurred_expenses_for_the_works and works_furthered_the_granted_purpose and grantor_knew_of_and_allowed_the_works and not right_to_revoke_was_reserved

predicates.is_claim_to_recover_property_from_licens: A claimant sought to recover property from a person occupying it with the owner’s permission.
predicates.permission_was_granted_for_a_continuing_: The owner permitted occupation of the property so the occupier could carry on an ongoing activity there.
predicates.licensee_made_permanent_works_on_the_pro: The permitted occupier constructed or carried out works of a permanent character on the property.
predicates.licensee_incurred_expenses_for_the_works: The permitted occupier spent money on the permanent works.
predicates.works_furthered_the_granted_purpose: The permanent works served the activity for which the owner had allowed occupation.
predicates.grantor_knew_of_and_allowed_the_works: The owner knew that the occupier was carrying out the works and did not object to them.
predicates.right_to_revoke_was_reserved: The parties did not reserve a right for the owner to revoke the permission.

issues.definition: Where permission for an ongoing purpose is acted on through permanent, costly works that further that purpose, and the owner knowingly allows them without reserving revocation, the permission cannot be revoked while the purpose continues.

issues.legal_issue: A family manager’s grant of a permanent licence is not invalid merely because the property belongs to a joint family where the licence transfers no title and the other family members do not challenge it.
material_facts: The property was found to belong to a joint family, and the former owner was its manager.
The former owner granted the school a permanent licence to use the premises, without transferring title to the school.
No co-sharer or other family member objected to the grant or to the school’s subsequent construction.
The record did not establish that the former owner’s minor sons were born before the licence was granted.
No co-sharer challenged the licence on the ground that the manager lacked authority.
issues.conclusion: The contention that the former owner lacked authority, as family manager, to grant the permanent licence was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that the grant was a licence rather than a transfer of title, that the family members had acquiesced in it, and that no co-sharer had challenged its validity. On these facts, the licence was not invalid merely because the grantor was the family manager; the Court cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.is_challenge_to_family_manager_granted_l: A party challenged permission granted over family property on the ground that the grantor acted as the family manager.
predicates.property_is_joint_family_property: The property belonged to a joint family.
predicates.manager_granted_permission_without_trans: The family manager permitted another person to use the property without transferring ownership to that person.
predicates.other_co_sharers_did_not_object_or_chall: The other family members neither objected to the permission nor challenged its validity.

issues.definition: A challenge based only on the grantor’s status as family manager does not invalidate permission over joint family property when title was not transferred and the other co-sharers did not object or challenge it.
